items.stem: What is the Avogadro constant?
options: the volume of one mole of gas at s.t.p.
the number of atoms in 1 kg of carbon-12
the mass of one mole of a substance
the number of particles in one mole of a substance
items.answer: the number of particles in one mole of a substance
items.markingKey: N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

items.stem: Explain why real gases deviate from ideal gas behaviour at high pressures and low temperatures.
items.answer: At high pressure the molecules are close together so their volume is not negligible; at low temperature they move slowly so intermolecular attractions become significant. Both assumptions of the ideal gas model fail.
items.markingKey: molecular volume significant at high p [1]; intermolecular forces significant at low T [1] [2]

items.stem: Show that pV = nRT can be written as pV = NkT.
items.answer: N = nN_A so n = N/N_A; pV = (N/N_A)RT = N(R/N_A)T = NkT.

items.stem: A cylinder of volume 2.50 × 10⁻² m³ contains oxygen at a pressure of 1.50 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 20 °C. Calculate the amount of gas in moles.
items.answer: 1.54 mol
items.markingKey: n = pV/(RT) = 1.50 × 10⁵ × 2.50 × 10⁻²/(8.31 × 293) = 1.54 mol. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A cylinder of volume 5.00 × 10⁻² m³ contains carbon dioxide at a pressure of 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 15 °C. Calculate the number of moles and the number of molecules of gas.

A steel gas cylinder of internal volume 0.010 m³ contains neon (molar mass 20.2 g mol⁻¹) at 1.00 × 10⁷ Pa and 20 °C. (a) Calculate the amount of gas in the cylinder. (b) The cylinder is left in the sun and warms to 45 °C. Calculate the new pressure.
items.markingKey: (a) n = pV/RT (method/substitution) [1]; answer 41.1 mol with unit [1] [2] (b) p ∝ T (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.09 × 10⁷ Pa [1] [2]

items.stem: How many molecules are there in 0.50 mol of oxygen?
Answer both parts. (a) An ideal gas is a gas that … (b) Which equation relates the Boltzmann constant k, molar gas constant R and Avogadro constant N_A?
items.answer: (a) obeys pV ∝ T at all pressures, volumes and temperatures (b) k = R/N_A
items.markingKey: (a) Ideal gases obey pV = nRT exactly. (b) pV = nRT = NkT with N = nN_A.

items.stem: Explain why the temperature in the ideal gas equation must be in kelvin.
items.answer: pV is proportional to the thermodynamic temperature, which is zero at absolute zero; using °C would give nonsensical results (e.g. zero or negative pV at 0 °C).
items.markingKey: p ∝ T only on absolute scale [1]; °C gives wrong/negative values [1] [2]

items.stem: A sealed rigid container of gas is heated. Explain why the pressure rises, using the ideal gas equation.
items.answer: n and V are constant, so p ∝ T: as T increases, p increases in proportion.
items.markingKey: n, V constant [1]; p ∝ T [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Show that pV = nRT can be written as pV = NkT. (b) A sealed rigid container of gas is heated. Explain why the pressure rises, using the ideal gas equation.
items.answer: (a) N = nN_A so n = N/N_A; pV = (N/N_A)RT = N(R/N_A)T = NkT. (b) n and V are constant, so p ∝ T: as T increases, p increases in proportion.
items.markingKey: (a) n = N/N_A [1]; k = R/N_A [1] [2] (b) n, V constant [1]; p ∝ T [1] [2]

items.stem: A car tyre in Muscat contains air at 2.80 × 10⁵ Pa at 10 °C. After a long drive the air is at 35 °C. Assume the volume of the tyre is constant. Calculate the new pressure.
items.markingKey: p₂ = p₁T₂/T₁ = 2.80 × 10⁵ × 308/283 = 3.05 × 10⁵ Pa. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A cylinder of volume 5.00 × 10⁻² m³ contains oxygen at a pressure of 2.00 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of −10 °C. Determine the amount of gas in moles.
items.answer: 4.58 mol
items.markingKey: n = pV/(RT) = 2.00 × 10⁵ × 5.00 × 10⁻²/(8.31 × 263) = 4.58 mol. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An aerosol can contains gas at 4.00 × 10⁵ Pa at 20 °C. It is thrown onto a bonfire and heated to 500 °C. Calculate the pressure at this temperature.
items.markingKey: p₂ = p₁T₂/T₁ = 4.00 × 10⁵ × 773/293 = 1.06 × 10⁶ Pa. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A cylinder of volume 5.00 × 10⁻³ m³ contains nitrogen at a pressure of 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 15 °C. The molar mass of nitrogen is 28 g mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate the amount of gas in moles. (b) Calculate the mass of gas. (c) Calculate the density of the gas.
A steel gas cylinder of internal volume 0.050 m³ contains oxygen (molar mass 32 g mol⁻¹) at 5.00 × 10⁶ Pa and 20 °C. (a) State what is meant by an ideal gas. (b) Calculate the mass of gas.
items.answer: (a) A gas that obeys pV ∝ T (pV = nRT) at all pressures, volumes and temperatures. (b) 3.29 kg
items.markingKey: (a) pV ∝ T [1]; at all p, V, T [1] [2] (b) m = nM: 3.29 kg [1]

items.stem: A steel gas cylinder of internal volume 0.050 m³ contains argon (molar mass 39.9 g mol⁻¹) at 5.00 × 10⁶ Pa and 20 °C. (a) State what is meant by an ideal gas. (b) The cylinder is left in the sun and warms to 45 °C. Calculate the new pressure.
items.answer: (a) A gas that obeys pV ∝ T (pV = nRT) at all pressures, volumes and temperatures. (b) 5.43 × 10⁶ Pa
items.markingKey: (a) pV ∝ T [1]; at all p, V, T [1] [2] (b) p ∝ T (method/substitution) [1]; answer 5.43 × 10⁶ Pa [1] [2]

items.stem: A steel gas cylinder of internal volume 0.010 m³ contains nitrogen (molar mass 28 g mol⁻¹) at 2.00 × 10⁵ Pa and 20 °C. (a) Calculate the amount of gas in the cylinder. (b) Calculate the mass of gas. (c) The cylinder is left in the sun and warms to 45 °C. Calculate the new pressure.
items.markingKey: (a) n = pV/RT (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.821 mol with unit [1] [2] (b) m = nM: 0.0230 kg [1] (c) p ∝ T (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.17 × 10⁵ Pa [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is an assumption of the kinetic theory of an ideal gas?
options: the molecules all move at the same speed
the volume of the molecules is large compared with the container
the collisions of the molecules are perfectly elastic
the molecules attract each other strongly
items.answer: the collisions of the molecules are perfectly elastic
items.markingKey: Kinetic energy is conserved in collisions.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of molecules, how a gas exerts a pressure on the walls of its container.
items.answer: Molecules collide with the walls and rebound, so their momentum changes; the wall exerts a force on each molecule and, by Newton's third law, the molecules exert a force on the wall. Many collisions per second give a steady force per unit area.
items.markingKey: momentum change on collision [1]; force on wall (N3), many collisions → pressure = force/area [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain, using kinetic theory, why the pressure of a gas increases when it is heated at constant volume.
items.answer: The molecules' mean speed increases, so they hit the walls more often and with greater change of momentum per collision; the rate of change of momentum (force) on the walls increases.
items.markingKey: higher speed [1]; more frequent and harder collisions → more force [1] [2]

items.stem: A sample of neon has density 0.347 kg m⁻³ at a pressure of 5.00 × 10⁴ Pa. Calculate the root-mean-square speed of the molecules.
items.answer: 657 m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: p = ⅓ρ⟨c²⟩ ⇒ c_rms = √(3p/ρ) = √(3 × 5.00 × 10⁴/0.347) = 657 m s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A sample of nitrogen has density 0.481 kg m⁻³ at a pressure of 5.00 × 10⁴ Pa. Use p = ⅓ρ⟨c²⟩ to calculate the mean-square speed and the root-mean-square speed of the molecules.
items.answer: ⟨c²⟩ = 3.12 × 10⁵ m² s⁻²; c_rms = 558 m s⁻¹

items.stem: A sample of hydrogen has density 0.138 kg m⁻³ at a pressure of 2.00 × 10⁵ Pa. (a) Show that p = ⅓ρ⟨c²⟩ follows from pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩. (b) Calculate the r.m.s. speed of the molecules. (c) The pressure is doubled at constant temperature. State and explain what happens to the r.m.s. speed.
items.answer: (a) ρ = Nm/V so p = ⅓(Nm/V)⟨c²⟩ = ⅓ρ⟨c²⟩ (b) 2090 m s⁻¹ (c) unchanged: ρ doubles too, so p/ρ is constant (c_rms depends only on T)
items.markingKey: (a) ρ = Nm/V [1] (b) c_rms = √(3p/ρ) [1]; = 2090 m s⁻¹ [1] (c) unchanged [1]; ρ doubles / depends only on T [1] [5]

items.stem: A single molecule of mass 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg moves with speed 500 m s⁻¹ back and forth perpendicular to two opposite walls of a cube of side 0.30 m, colliding elastically. (a) Calculate the time between successive collisions with the same wall. (b) Explain how this model is extended to give pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩.
items.answer: (a) 1.20 × 10⁻³ s (b) N molecules with random velocities: use mean-square speed, and ⟨cₓ²⟩ = ⅓⟨c²⟩ for each direction; pressure = force/area with V = L³.
items.markingKey: (a) t = 2L/c: 1.20 × 10⁻³ s [1] (b) N molecules and ⟨c²⟩ [1]; factor ⅓ from three directions [1]; p = F/L² and V = L³ [1] [3]

items.stem: A single molecule of mass 4.65 × 10⁻²⁶ kg moves with speed 400 m s⁻¹ back and forth perpendicular to two opposite walls of a cube of side 0.20 m, colliding elastically. (a) Calculate the change in momentum of the molecule in one collision with a wall. (b) Calculate the time between successive collisions with the same wall. (c) Calculate the mean force exerted on the wall by this molecule.
items.markingKey: (a) Δp = 2mc (method/substitution) [1]; answer 3.72 × 10⁻²³ N s [1] [2] (b) t = 2L/c: 1.00 × 10⁻³ s [1] (c) F = Δp/t = mc²/L (method/substitution) [1]; answer 3.72 × 10⁻²⁰ N [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is an assumption of the kinetic model of an ideal gas?
options: there are forces between molecules at all times
the time spent in collisions is negligible compared with the time between collisions
the molecules move in ordered layers
the molecules are at rest between collisions
items.answer: the time spent in collisions is negligible compared with the time between collisions
items.markingKey: Collisions are instantaneous.

items.stem: In pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩, what does ⟨c²⟩ represent?
options: the speed of the fastest molecule squared
the square of the mean speed
the mean of the squares of the speeds of the molecules
items.answer: the mean of the squares of the speeds of the molecules
items.markingKey: Mean square speed.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Four molecules have speeds 1, 2, 3 and 4 (in units of 100 m s⁻¹). What is their root-mean-square speed? (b) Gas molecules hit a container wall. The pressure on the wall is due to …
items.answer: (a) 274 m s⁻¹ (b) the rate of change of momentum of the molecules at the wall
items.markingKey: (a) √((1 + 4 + 9 + 16)/4) × 100 = √7.5 × 100. (b) Force = rate of change of momentum; pressure = force/area.

items.stem: A molecule of mass m moving at speed c perpendicular to a wall rebounds elastically. Show that its change in momentum is 2mc and explain how this leads to the force on the wall.
items.answer: Momentum changes from +mc to −mc: Δp = 2mc. In a cube of side L the time between hits on the same wall is 2L/c, so the mean force = 2mc ÷ (2L/c) = mc²/L.
items.markingKey: Δp = 2mc [1]; time 2L/c so F = mc²/L [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the factor ⅓ appears in pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩.
items.answer: Molecules move randomly in three dimensions; on average ⟨c²⟩ = ⟨cₓ²⟩ + ⟨c_y²⟩ + ⟨c_z²⟩ with the three equal, so ⟨cₓ²⟩ = ⅓⟨c²⟩ for the direction perpendicular to a wall.
items.markingKey: random motion, three equal components [1]; ⟨cₓ²⟩ = ⅓⟨c²⟩ [1] [2]

(b) Molecules collide with the walls and rebound, so their momentum changes; the wall exerts a force on each molecule and, by Newton's third law, the molecules exert a force on the wall. Many collisions per second give a steady force per unit area.

items.answer: ⟨c²⟩ = 3.70 × 10⁵ m² s⁻²; c_rms = 609 m s⁻¹

items.stem: Which expression gives the mean translational kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas at thermodynamic temperature T?
items.answer: 3kT/2
items.markingKey: ½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT.

items.stem: Use pV = NkT and pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩ to show that the mean kinetic energy of a molecule is (3/2)kT.
items.answer: Equate: ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩ = NkT, so m⟨c²⟩ = 3kT and ½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT.
items.markingKey: equate the two expressions [1]; rearrange to ½m⟨c²⟩ = 3kT/2 [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why, at the same temperature, the molecules of hydrogen move faster on average than the molecules of nitrogen.
items.answer: At the same T the mean KE ½m⟨c²⟩ is the same; hydrogen molecules have smaller mass, so their mean-square speed must be larger.
items.markingKey: same mean KE at same T [1]; smaller m so larger speed [1] [2]

items.stem: A sample of nitrogen (molar mass 28 g mol⁻¹) is at a temperature of 100 °C. Calculate the mean translational kinetic energy of a molecule.

items.stem: A mixture of nitrogen (molar mass 28 g mol⁻¹) and argon (molar mass 39.9 g mol⁻¹) is at 300 K. (a) Calculate the mean kinetic energy of a molecule of each gas. (b) Calculate the ratio of the r.m.s. speed of nitrogen to that of argon.
items.answer: (a) 6.21 × 10⁻²¹ J for both (b) 1.19

items.stem: What is the mean kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas at 300 K?
Explain what the thermodynamic temperature of a gas represents at the molecular level.
items.answer: It is proportional to the mean random (translational) kinetic energy of the molecules.
items.markingKey: proportional to mean KE [1]; random motion [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why some light molecules such as hydrogen can escape from the Earth's atmosphere although the mean speed is well below the escape speed.
items.answer: There is a distribution of speeds; a small fraction of hydrogen molecules (which have high mean speed because of their small mass) have speeds above escape speed and are lost over time.
items.markingKey: distribution of speeds [1]; some exceed escape speed, more likely for light molecules [1] [2]

items.stem: A sample of a noble gas is studied in a laboratory. The thermodynamic temperature is multiplied by 4 while the mass of a molecule stays the same. State and explain how the r.m.s. speed of the molecules changes.
items.answer: The r.m.s. speed of the molecules doubles.

items.stem: An ideal gas is trapped in a cylinder by a piston. The amount of gas is doubled while the thermodynamic temperature and volume stay the same. State and explain how the pressure of the gas changes.
items.answer: The pressure of the gas doubles.
items.markingKey: Using pV = nRT: pressure of the gas ∝ amount of gas; factor = 2.00 = 2.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A cylinder of volume 2.00 × 10⁻³ m³ contains nitrogen at a pressure of 1.20 × 10⁶ Pa and a temperature of 15 °C. Work out the amount of gas in moles.
items.answer: 1.00 mol
items.markingKey: n = pV/(RT) = 1.20 × 10⁶ × 2.00 × 10⁻³/(8.31 × 288) = 1.00 mol. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An aerosol can contains gas at 4.00 × 10⁵ Pa at 20 °C. It is thrown onto a bonfire and heated to 300 °C. Work out the pressure at this temperature.
items.markingKey: p₂ = p₁T₂/T₁ = 4.00 × 10⁵ × 573/293 = 7.82 × 10⁵ Pa. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [3]

items.stem: A steel gas cylinder of internal volume 0.020 m³ contains oxygen (molar mass 32 g mol⁻¹) at 1.00 × 10⁷ Pa and 20 °C. (a) State what is meant by an ideal gas. (b) Calculate the amount of gas in the cylinder.
items.answer: (a) A gas that obeys pV ∝ T (pV = nRT) at all pressures, volumes and temperatures. (b) 82.1 mol
items.markingKey: (a) pV ∝ T [1]; at all p, V, T [1] [2] (b) n = pV/RT (method/substitution) [1]; answer 82.1 mol with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Which expression gives the pressure of an ideal gas of density ρ?
items.answer: ⅓ρ⟨c²⟩
items.markingKey: p = ⅓(Nm/V)⟨c²⟩ = ⅓ρ⟨c²⟩.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain, in terms of molecules, how a gas exerts a pressure on the walls of its container. (b) Explain why the factor ⅓ appears in pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩.
items.answer: (a) Molecules collide with the walls and rebound, so their momentum changes; the wall exerts a force on each molecule and, by Newton's third law, the molecules exert a force on the wall. Many collisions per second give a steady force per unit area. (b) Molecules move randomly in three dimensions; on average ⟨c²⟩ = ⟨cₓ²⟩ + ⟨c_y²⟩ + ⟨c_z²⟩ with the three equal, so ⟨cₓ²⟩ = ⅓⟨c²⟩ for the direction perpendicular to a wall.
items.markingKey: (a) momentum change on collision [1]; force on wall (N3), many collisions → pressure = force/area [1] [2] (b) random motion, three equal components [1]; ⟨cₓ²⟩ = ⅓⟨c²⟩ [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the factor ⅓ appears in pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩. (b) Explain, using kinetic theory, why the pressure of a gas increases when it is heated at constant volume.
items.answer: (a) Molecules move randomly in three dimensions; on average ⟨c²⟩ = ⟨cₓ²⟩ + ⟨c_y²⟩ + ⟨c_z²⟩ with the three equal, so ⟨cₓ²⟩ = ⅓⟨c²⟩ for the direction perpendicular to a wall. (b) The molecules' mean speed increases, so they hit the walls more often and with greater change of momentum per collision; the rate of change of momentum (force) on the walls increases.
items.markingKey: (a) random motion, three equal components [1]; ⟨cₓ²⟩ = ⅓⟨c²⟩ [1] [2] (b) higher speed [1]; more frequent and harder collisions → more force [1] [2]

items.stem: In a model, the molecules of a gas have speeds of 300, 400, 600, 800 m s⁻¹. Calculate the mean speed, the mean-square speed and the root-mean-square speed.
items.answer: mean = 525 m s⁻¹; ⟨c²⟩ = 3.12 × 10⁵ m² s⁻²; c_rms = 559 m s⁻¹

items.stem: A sample of nitrogen has density 1.01 kg m⁻³ at a pressure of 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa. Work out the root-mean-square speed of the molecules.
items.answer: 597 m s⁻¹

items.stem: A single molecule of mass 4.65 × 10⁻²⁶ kg moves with speed 1200 m s⁻¹ back and forth perpendicular to two opposite walls of a cube of side 0.30 m, colliding elastically. (a) Calculate the mean force exerted on the wall by this molecule. (b) State two assumptions of the kinetic theory used in this derivation.
items.answer: (a) 2.23 × 10⁻¹⁹ N (b) Elastic collisions; no intermolecular forces; negligible molecular volume; collision time negligible.
items.markingKey: (a) F = Δp/t = mc²/L (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.23 × 10⁻¹⁹ N [1] [2] (b) first valid assumption [1]; second valid assumption [1] [2]

items.stem: A single molecule of mass 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg moves with speed 500 m s⁻¹ back and forth perpendicular to two opposite walls of a cube of side 0.30 m, colliding elastically. (a) Calculate the change in momentum of the molecule in one collision with a wall. (b) Calculate the time between successive collisions with the same wall. (c) Calculate the mean force exerted on the wall by this molecule.
items.markingKey: (a) Δp = 2mc (method/substitution) [1]; answer 6.64 × 10⁻²⁴ N s [1] [2] (b) t = 2L/c: 1.20 × 10⁻³ s [1] (c) F = Δp/t = mc²/L (method/substitution) [1]; answer 5.53 × 10⁻²¹ N [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) At what temperature would the mean kinetic energy of the molecules of an ideal gas be zero (classically)? (b) State the relationship between the mean kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas and its thermodynamic temperature.
items.answer: (a) 0 K (b) ½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT: mean KE is proportional to T.
items.markingKey: (a) Mean KE ∝ T. (b) ½m⟨c²⟩ = 3kT/2 [1]

items.stem: A sample of a noble gas is studied in a laboratory. The mass of a molecule is doubled while the thermodynamic temperature stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the r.m.s. speed of the molecules changes.
items.answer: The r.m.s. speed of the molecules is multiplied by 0.707.
items.markingKey: Using ½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT: r.m.s. speed of the molecules ∝ mass of a molecule^-0.500; factor = 2.00^-0.500 = 0.707. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why some light molecules such as hydrogen can escape from the Earth's atmosphere although the mean speed is well below the escape speed. (b) Explain why, at the same temperature, the molecules of hydrogen move faster on average than the molecules of nitrogen.
items.answer: (a) There is a distribution of speeds; a small fraction of hydrogen molecules (which have high mean speed because of their small mass) have speeds above escape speed and are lost over time. (b) At the same T the mean KE ½m⟨c²⟩ is the same; hydrogen molecules have smaller mass, so their mean-square speed must be larger.
items.markingKey: (a) distribution of speeds [1]; some exceed escape speed, more likely for light molecules [1] [2] (b) same mean KE at same T [1]; smaller m so larger speed [1] [2]

items.stem: A container holds 0.20 mol of helium (a monatomic ideal gas) at 100 °C. Calculate the total kinetic energy of all the atoms.
items.markingKey: N = nN_A [1]; mean KE = 3kT/2 [1]; total = N × 3kT/2 = (3/2)nRT = 930 J [1] [3]

items.stem: A mixture of neon (molar mass 20.2 g mol⁻¹) and nitrogen (molar mass 28 g mol⁻¹) is at 280 K. (a) Show that the mean kinetic energy of a molecule is (3/2)kT. (b) Calculate the mean kinetic energy of a molecule of each gas. (c) Calculate the ratio of the r.m.s. speed of neon to that of nitrogen.
items.answer: (a) ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩ = NkT ⇒ ½m⟨c²⟩ = 3kT/2. (b) 5.80 × 10⁻²¹ J for both (c) 1.18
items.markingKey: (a) equate expressions [1]; rearrange [1] [2] (b) same for both (method/substitution) [1]; answer 5.80 × 10⁻²¹ J for both [1] [2] (c) √(M_b/M_a) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.18 [1] [2]

items.stem: A fixed mass of ideal gas has its thermodynamic temperature doubled at constant volume. What happens to the pressure?
options: it increases by a factor of 4
items.answer: it doubles
items.markingKey: p ∝ T at constant V and n.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the temperature in the ideal gas equation must be in kelvin. (b) Explain why real gases deviate from ideal gas behaviour at high pressures and low temperatures.
items.answer: (a) pV is proportional to the thermodynamic temperature, which is zero at absolute zero; using °C would give nonsensical results (e.g. zero or negative pV at 0 °C). (b) At high pressure the molecules are close together so their volume is not negligible; at low temperature they move slowly so intermolecular attractions become significant. Both assumptions of the ideal gas model fail.
items.markingKey: (a) p ∝ T only on absolute scale [1]; °C gives wrong/negative values [1] [2] (b) molecular volume significant at high p [1]; intermolecular forces significant at low T [1] [2]

items.stem: A sealed balloon of ideal gas is studied. The volume is multiplied by 4 while the thermodynamic temperature and amount of gas stay the same. Predict, with a reason, how the pressure of the gas changes.
items.answer: The pressure of the gas becomes a quarter.
items.markingKey: Using pV = nRT: pressure of the gas ∝ volume^-1.00; factor = 4.00^-1.00 = 0.250. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

the kinetic energy lost in collisions
items.answer: the rate of change of momentum of the molecules at the wall
items.markingKey: Force = rate of change of momentum; pressure = force/area.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A molecule of mass m moving at speed c perpendicular to a wall rebounds elastically. Show that its change in momentum is 2mc and explain how this leads to the force on the wall. (b) Explain why the factor ⅓ appears in pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩.
items.answer: (a) Momentum changes from +mc to −mc: Δp = 2mc. In a cube of side L the time between hits on the same wall is 2L/c, so the mean force = 2mc ÷ (2L/c) = mc²/L. (b) Molecules move randomly in three dimensions; on average ⟨c²⟩ = ⟨cₓ²⟩ + ⟨c_y²⟩ + ⟨c_z²⟩ with the three equal, so ⟨cₓ²⟩ = ⅓⟨c²⟩ for the direction perpendicular to a wall.
items.markingKey: (a) Δp = 2mc [1]; time 2L/c so F = mc²/L [1] [2] (b) random motion, three equal components [1]; ⟨cₓ²⟩ = ⅓⟨c²⟩ [1] [2]

Many collisions per second give a steady force per unit area. (b) Momentum changes from +mc to −mc: Δp = 2mc. In a cube of side L the time between hits on the same wall is 2L/c, so the mean force = 2mc ÷ (2L/c) = mc²/L.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Use pV = NkT and pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩ to show that the mean kinetic energy of a molecule is (3/2)kT. (b) Explain what the thermodynamic temperature of a gas represents at the molecular level.
items.answer: (a) Equate: ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩ = NkT, so m⟨c²⟩ = 3kT and ½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT. (b) It is proportional to the mean random (translational) kinetic energy of the molecules.
